items.title: Refresh benchmark results and fix the broken benchmark runner
items.body:
Se corrió la campaña completa de benchmarks porque la última era del 1 de julio y desde entonces entraron cambios que afectan los números, en particular `im2col` cache-friendly y el fix de gradientes de max-pooling.

Para poder correrla hubo que arreglar dos cosas que estaban rotas en `main`:

- `make dataset` apuntaba a `scripts/download_mnist.sh`, que el PR #218 eliminó al reemplazarlo por la versión en Python.
- `gen_compose.py` leía `PUMBA` con `os.environ[...]` sin default. El PR #216 la agregó como obligatoria y actualizó `docker/compose_up.py`, pero no `benchmarks/issue/runner.py`. Por eso toda generación de compose desde el runner fallaba con `KeyError: 'PUMBA'`.

El segundo dejó el benchmark inutilizable desde el 25 de julio. No se detectó antes porque el CI solo corre `cargo test`.

## Resultados

Campaña con `--fresh --repeats 3`, misma parametrización que la del 1 de julio. 38 configuraciones, ninguna con error, 2 h 37 min contra las 5 h 39 min anteriores.

Comparando clave por clave contra la corrida archivada:

| Métrica | Resultado |
|---|---|
| Tiempo de entrenamiento (mediana) | -58,2 % |
| Exactitud | sin cambios |
| Línea de base de PyTorch | -1,2 % y +3,9 % |

La línea de base de PyTorch funciona como control: no cambió entre las dos corridas, así que la mejora no se explica por el estado de la máquina sino por el código. Una mediana de -58,2 % equivale a un speedup de 2,39x, consistente con el 2,27x que se le atribuye a la optimización de convolución.

La exactitud queda idéntica a cuatro decimales en casi todas las configuraciones.

## Alcance

Actualiza `benchmarks/README.md`, `benchmarks/plots/` y los resultados. No toca el informe: los números del Estudio I salen de otro arnés y sobre FashionMNIST, que este runner no cubre.

fix(benchmarks): publish results via a PR so they reach the tutorial
items.body:
The Benchmarks workflow ran fine but its results never reached the published tutorial. I traced it to three compounding bugs, all confirmed from the run logs.

## Why the results weren't loading

**1. Manual runs never published.** The Commit/Deploy steps were gated on `github.event_name == 'schedule'`. Your most recent run (`workflow_dispatch` on master, 9h ago) succeeded and refreshed the docs *in the runner*, but those steps show `skipped` — the results were thrown away:

```
success  Run CI-safe benchmarks ... update docs
skipped  Commit refreshed benchmark results
skipped  Deploy docs
```

**2. Scheduled runs' push is rejected by branch protection.** The weekly run *did* commit and try to push to `master`, but:

```
[master 3eb694f] chore(benchmarks): refresh published benchmark results
 1 file changed, 32 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
remote: error: GH006: Protected branch update failed for refs/heads/master.
 ! [remote rejected] master -> master (protected branch hook declined)
```

`git push || echo ...` masked the rejection, so the step falsely "succeeded" and the numbers never reached source.

**3. The one-off `gh-deploy` is transient.** The workflow also ran its own `mkdocs gh-deploy` to `tutorial-gh-pages`. But `release-docs.yml` redeploys from the (still-placeholder) master **source** on the next master push and overwrites it — which is exactly why the live tutorial reads *"No benchmark results published yet."*

## The fix

Stop force-pushing to protected `master` and stop the one-off deploy. Instead **open (or roll forward) a PR** with the refreshed `parameter-identification.md`. Merging it lands the numbers in source and triggers `release-docs.yml`, which republishes from source so the table **persists**.

- Gated on `github.ref == 'refs/heads/master'` (not the trigger) → works for both the weekly schedule **and** manual dispatch on master; a `run-benchmarks-*` tag on a feature branch still just emails/summarises.
- Publishes regardless of the `--assert` outcome — a cost/timing regression is a real number worth publishing; the assertion failure still turns the job red and shows in the summary/email.
- `add-paths` keeps the PR to the docs file only; a single rolling branch (`benchmarks/refresh-results`) means one PR, not one per run.
- Adds `pull-requests: write`. Documents the bypass-token option if you want fully hands-off publishing (the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` can't bypass branch protection).

## What you do now

Trigger **Benchmarks** (or wait for the weekly run) → it opens a **"chore(benchmarks): refresh published benchmark results"** PR → merge it → the tutorial updates and stays updated.

For fully automatic weekly publishing with no merge, either grant `github-actions[bot]` bypass on the branch-protection rule, or set a PAT/App token as `token:` on the PR step (noted in a comment).

> Note: I couldn't exercise GitHub Actions locally — the YAML is validated and the logic verified against the run logs, but the first real confirmation is the next Benchmarks run opening the PR.

items.body:
## Summary
- The `benchmark.yml` workflow's "Run Benchmarks" job has failed on every `pull_request`-triggered run for months (confirmed across unrelated dependabot PRs going back to April) — it only ever "worked" on `push` to `main`, which skips the affected step entirely.
- Root cause: the `run_benchmark` step sets its `results_file` output while the shell is `cd`'d into `benchmarks/`, so the value is relative to that directory (e.g. `results/benchmark_results_*.json`). The "Compare with baseline" step also `cd`s into `benchmarks` first, so it already resolves this correctly. The "Comment on PR" step does not `cd`, so it read the same output value directly from the workspace root and failed with `ENOENT`.
- Fix: resolve the path relative to `benchmarks/` in the one step that doesn't already `cd` there, rather than changing the output's meaning (which the already-working "Compare with baseline" step depends on).

Found while investigating an unrelated PR (#36) that surfaced this as a "Benchmarks action failed" report — confirmed via `gh run list --workflow=benchmark.yml --event=pull_request` that this branch's changes aren't the cause; this workflow file was untouched by that branch.

It now renders comparison, magnitude, signed percentage-point delta, and relative performance in the answer language. Historical stored phrases are normalized back into typed facts before rendering.

items.title: fix(rl): record benchmark results for candidates measured cross-provider
items.body:
## Defect

`record_benchmark_result` looked up a candidate with `_find_candidate` — exact `(section, provider)` key, **no fallback** — while the *serving* path (`optimization_injector`) falls back to `find_candidate_any_provider`. So a candidate evolved under one provider but measured under another was:

- **served correctly** — its text injected, the measurement valid; then
- **silently un-recordable** — `_find_candidate` finds nothing under the run provider → `record_benchmark_result` returns None → `recorded=False` → `decision.passed = passed AND recorded = False`.

Every cross-provider benchmark (all of them in practice: candidates evolve under whichever provider has quota, are benchmarked under whichever has it now) reported **"no candidate met the threshold"** on results that cleared the gate.

## Discovery

An n=60 mbpp run measured a **+9/60 winner** — `b54762402bda` vs seed, disc 14/5, effect 9 over a √19 = 4.36 noise floor, p=0.06 — and reported "no candidate met the threshold." The candidate is stored under `provider=moonshot`; the run was `provider=deepseek`. Serving resolved it (valid +9/60); recording could not. Verified empirically:

```
_candidates has key GROUNDING_RULES::moonshot ? True
_candidates has key GROUNDING_RULES::deepseek ? False
RECORDING  _find_candidate(deepseek):  False   <- no fallback -> None -> recorded=False
SERVING    any_provider fallback:      True    <- measurement valid
```

Same defect class as the self-inflicted prompt-injection work: the framework classifies its own candidates by provider and then cannot attribute measurements that cross that boundary.

## Fix

`record_benchmark_result` falls back to `find_candidate_any_provider` when the provider-specific lookup misses — matching serving. One consistent resolution path for both.

## Verification (TDD, mutation-checked)

- New `TestCrossProviderRecording` in `test_comparative_gate.py`: pins the direct recording call **and** the end-to-end gate verdict (a +6-effect winner stored under moonshot, measured under deepseek, must be recorded and approved).
- **Red**: both fail before the fix (`passed=False, recorded=False` despite `variant_only_pass=6, baseline_only_pass=0`).
- **Green**: both pass after.
- **Mutation**: reverting the fallback re-fails both (tests genuinely guard the behavior, not vacuously pass).
- No regression: 14/14 gate suite + 112/112 across `test_prompt_optimizer`, `test_prompt_reward_loop_closes`, `test_optimization_injector_binding`, `test_paired_contrast`. black/ruff/mypy clean.

The +9/60 result that surfaced this is recoverable from the run artifacts; the corrected gate now lets such a result be recorded and evaluated on its merits.

items.title: fix(benchmark): preserve gateway and results through restoration
items.body:
Fixes #26

## Root cause

Hermes Local treated Hermes Agent's persisted gateway `updated_at` value as a periodic heartbeat. It is actually updated when gateway/platform state changes. A healthy idle gateway therefore eventually appeared stale even though:

- the authoritative gateway PID was live;
- the runtime record still matched that process;
- the gateway state was `running`;
- Discord remained `connected`.

During a benchmark, the 60-second grace expired before the native cases and model reload completed. The supervisor then declared the connected gateway unhealthy, exited during restoration, and discarded the completed in-memory benchmark cases.

## Fix

- Derive gateway health from authoritative process identity, gateway state, and enabled platform states.
- Keep runtime timestamp age as advisory diagnostic metadata instead of a liveness gate.
- Continue failing closed for missing/dead gateway processes, mismatched runtime identity, disconnected/fatal platforms, and duplicate logical roots.
- Checkpoint native benchmark results and a report before releasing the model lease.
- Join or start a replacement supervisor if the original controller exits during restoration.
- Record whether replacement-supervisor recovery was required in the result lifecycle metadata.
- Bump the local manifest to `0.18.3`.

## Portability

The change does not assume a GPU vendor, model, profile, context size, benchmark duration, gateway platform, or fixed workstation speed. It uses lifecycle and process/state contracts rather than extending a hardware-dependent timeout.

## Tests

- Stale timestamp + live matching PID + connected platform remains healthy.
- Dead/mismatched process and disconnected platform remain unhealthy.
- Deprecated stale-grace values do not alter health.
- Benchmark contract requires pre-restoration result checkpointing and replacement-supervisor recovery.
- Existing benchmark portability self-test remains part of the Windows validation job.

items.title: Fix trace replay JSONB metric merge

## What changed

- Bind reconstructed full-response metrics as a JSONB object instead of a string.
- Update the trace replay regression test to require an object parameter and reject double encoding.

## Why

Historical AgentX artifacts need full-response metrics reconstructed from retained profiles. Passing the patch through `JSON.stringify` stored it as a JSON string; PostgreSQL JSONB concatenation then converted `benchmark_results.metrics` from an object into an array, causing chart metrics to fall back to zero.

This preserves backward compatibility for historical artifacts while leaving current artifacts unchanged.

## Validation

Further testing was skipped at request for a quick PR.

items.title: 🐛 fix benchmark submit gateway url and results rendering
items.body:
## Summary

Five defects in the benchmark feature (PACT-756, https://linear.app/pact-toolkit/issue/PACT-756), plus a mock-data fix to keep the mock experience consistent with the real contract:

1. **Gateway URL fallback** - `BenchmarkWorkbench.tsx` fell back to `http://localhost:8080` (pact-auth's port) when `NEXT_PUBLIC_PACT_GATEWAY_URL` was unset, instead of the gateway's `:8110`. This is why a real 180-row run against a real backend errored on every single row. Fallback corrected to `:8110`. Audited every file under `env/`:
   - `env/local-real.env`: added `NEXT_PUBLIC_PACT_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8110` right after the existing `PACT_GATEWAY_URL` line (matches the value already in that file).
   - `env/demo.env`: added `NEXT_PUBLIC_PACT_GATEWAY_URL` matching its existing `PACT_GATEWAY_URL` (`https://api-demo.pact.example.com`).
   - `env/local.env`: corrected the stale `PACT_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080` to `:8110`. Did **not** add `NEXT_PUBLIC_PACT_GATEWAY_URL` here - `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_MOCKING=enabled` means MSW intercepts every request in this env, so the client-side gateway URL is never read.

2. **isRowCorrect label mismatch** - compared `expected_label` against `'hostile'`/`'safe'`, but the gateway/pact-benchmark contract (verified against `pact-benchmark`'s `runner/corpus.py` and `runner/runner.py`) only ever produces lowercase `'allow'`/`'block'`. Every real-backend row was silently marked incorrect. Fixed to compare against the real contract values. The generated `BenchmarkJobRowBody.expected_label` type is a plain `string` (not a narrowed union), so no codegen type needed changing.

3. **Client corpus validation** - `validateCorpusFile` checked column presence but never validated label values. Added value validation (case-insensitive, matching the backend's lowercase-then-check behavior in `corpus.py`) across every row, not just the first. On violation, the error names the offending row number and the bad value, e.g. `Row 3: expected_label must be "allow" or "block", got "hostile"`.

4. **Per-row error rendering** - the results table rendered an "error" chip for the Decision column but never the row's `error` message string, making failed rows undiagnosable from the UI. Added a quiet (`text-xs text-muted-foreground`), truncated `Error` column with a `title` tooltip carrying the full message; empty when the row has no error.

5. **Run-comparison select overflow** - long run labels overflowed the Baseline/Candidate `<select>` elements horizontally out of the card. Added `min-w-0` to the flex parents and `max-w-full truncate` to both selects so long labels ellipsize inside the card instead of overflowing it.

6. **Mock data followed the old vocabulary** - `MOCK_ROWS` in `src/app/benchmark/mock/data/benchmark.ts` seeded `expected_label` as `hostile`/`safe`, the same wrong vocabulary `isRowCorrect` used to compare against. Once #2 above fixed `isRowCorrect` to check the real `allow`/`block` contract, every mock-mode row started rendering "Incorrect" (previously masked because both sides agreed on the wrong vocabulary). Reseeded `MOCK_ROWS` to `allow`/`block` (safe -> allow, hostile -> block), keeping the same correct/incorrect row pattern (every 7th row deliberately wrong) so the Correct column shows a realistic mix again.

## Verification

**Gates** (from a fresh clone, branch off master, re-run after the mock-data commit):
- `tsc --noEmit` - pass
- `eslint .` - pass
- `TZ=CET vitest run` - 626 tests passed (77 files), including 15 new tests in `src/app/benchmark/test/benchmark_job.test.ts` covering the isRowCorrect allow/block/error matrix and validateCorpusFile's bad-label-value/case-insensitivity/valid-file paths for both JSONL and CSV
- `next build` - pass

**Mock-mode E2E** (`env/local.env` via `PORT=3910 pnpm run dev:mock`, driven with a throwaway Playwright script, deleted afterward):
- `/benchmark` loaded cleanly, no console errors
- Run comparison card: with the seeded mock run labels (e.g. `stub · seed-v2.jsonl · v0.5.0 · 22 Jul 2026`), `document.body.scrollWidth` equaled `window.innerWidth` (1280px) - no horizontal overflow, confirmed by screenshot
- Submitted a corpus through the upload form; the mock job progressed to done and the per-row results table rendered with the new `Error` column present in the header, `Expected`/`Decision` values as `allow`/`block`, and the Correct column showing a realistic mix (17 correct / 3 incorrect across the first page of 20 rows) instead of all-incorrect

items.title: Fix benchmark alignment and publish L40S/BABILong results
items.body:
## What changed

- replace instruction-style retrieval generation with checkpoint-exact, teacher-forced scoring through the training model
- pair retrieval fixtures across lengths and depths, report token accuracy/exact match/NLL, and clear CUDA allocations between long-context examples
- add 4K and 16K evaluation points, retain direct evaluation through 256K, and cap paged serving at the validated 128K limit
- add controlled BABILong answer-only fine-tuning on 0K/1K/2K with disjoint train, validation, and held-out test rows
- add a checkpoint-exact full-recompute BABILong generation backend that reaches 262,144 tokens without silent truncation or paged KV-cache dependence
- add a resumable all-checkpoint BABILong train/pilot/eval/Hub-upload pipeline with immutable source and dataset revisions
- make BABILong aggregation protocol-safe, preserve OOM cells, and report per-task plus complete-task macro accuracy
- fix one-slot inference warmup and resumable log completion detection
- update PIQA, Proof-Pile, and FinePDF loading for the installed datasets runtime
- publish the original L40S raw log bundle and document both the no-fine-tune matrix and audited BABILong result tables
- link the five public fine-tuned Hugging Face checkpoints and document matched-versus-confounded interpretation

## Why

The prior retrieval path reused the paged serving engine across cells and evaluated base checkpoints with instruction-style free generation. This produced uniformly zero scores and eventually triggered illegal CUDA memory accesses during sequential long-context sweeps. The corrected protocol follows the direct-forward semantics used by scaled_ablation/eval_hf_checkpoints.py.

BABILong requires matched task adaptation rather than zero-shot base-model generation. The new protocol teaches only the task format at contexts up to 2K, then measures held-out length extrapolation through exactly 256K while pinning the tokenizer, prompts, dataset revision, and row split.

## Impact

The five promoted checkpoints now complete paired retrieval and long-document scoring through 256K without CUDA corruption. BABILong adds a controlled adapted-reasoning comparison: at 256K, Polar reaches 28% macro accuracy versus 14% for RoPE and 0% for NoPE in the matched Atma+Muon group. Raven Native reaches 46% and Atma Raven Titans 38%, reported separately because their model family and optimizer differ.

All five fine-tuned checkpoints were uploaded publicly under ChavyvAkvar/atma-10b-babilong-2k-ft-*. Generated BABILong logs and multi-gigabyte local checkpoints are ignored so they cannot be staged accidentally; structured values and interpretation are recorded in benchmarks/README.md.

## Validation

- python -m tests.verify --cuda: 30 passed, 0 failed
- latest benchmark pipeline unit suite: 25 passed
- full original L40S benchmark run: 30/30 jobs complete, no OOM or illegal-access cells
- BABILong: 5/5 fine-tunes, 5/5 256K pilots, and 5/5 full sweeps complete
- BABILong coverage: 5,000 held-out responses across 10 tasks, 10 lengths, and 5 models
- BABILong GPU-stage time: 7h11m; no OOM, unsupported, missing, or null cells
- rebuilt BABILong aggregate: 550 rows, exactly equal to the saved matrix
- every README BABILong macro and per-task table cell checked programmatically against the aggregate
- five public Hugging Face repositories and uploaded commit IDs verified against the Hub

items.title: Enable experimental Vector scanner on JDK 21+
items.body:
## Summary

- remove the JDK 26 MR-JAR layout and compile the experimental Vector scanner into the Java 21 base artifact
- keep `jdk.incubator.vector` out of SafeRE's public module descriptor; explicit Vector activation adds the runtime read edge dynamically after the user supplies `--add-modules=jdk.incubator.vector`
- replace the JDK 24-only unsigned comparison operator with equivalent Java 21-compatible `GE`/`LE` Vector comparisons
- standardize production and release builds on JDK 26 with `--release 21`
- compile production and Vector test artifacts once on JDK 26, then run those exact artifacts with Vector enabled on JDK 21 through 26 in CI
- add a no-build benchmark mode for exercising the same JDK 26-built artifact across supported runtime JDKs

Fixes #658

## Benchmark results

The production-provider end-to-end benchmark ran sequentially in both SWAR and Vector modes on JDK 21 through 26, using the same JDK 26-built Java 21 artifact. Across 16 eligible pair/range trials, the geometric mean of Vector/SWAR time was:

| Runtime | Vector / SWAR | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|
| JDK 21 | 0.215 | 4.64x faster |
| JDK 22 | 0.232 | 4.30x faster |
| JDK 23 | 0.231 | 4.34x faster |
| JDK 24 | 0.230 | 4.34x faster |
| JDK 25 | 0.232 | 4.32x faster |
| JDK 26 | 0.227 | 4.40x faster |

Long absent/late scans improved by roughly 7.6x to 8.5x. Early-match sparse/dense cases improved by roughly 1.25x to 1.29x overall; dense matches were generally neutral, including one JDK 22 trial about 1.1% slower.

The broader 23-workload benchmark set, whose shared module requires JDK 22 because of its FFM engine, also ran sequentially on JDK 22 through 26. Its Vector/SWAR geometric-mean ratios were 0.617, 0.617, 0.617, 0.620, and 0.614 respectively. Long confirmation runs found the close dense-range, ASCII-range, and fixed-offset results neutral within their uncertainty.

After rebasing onto the multi-range Vector implementation, a controlled comparison measured the Java 21-compatible `GE`/`LE` implementation against `ULE`. The standard run covered 120 paired results across JDK 24 through 26 and produced a 0.9990 geometric-mean GE/LE-to-ULE ratio. A long confirmation covered 36 paired scan-heavy results and produced a 0.9988 ratio. Every long-run pair had overlapping 99.9% confidence intervals, so the compatible implementation has no measurable performance cost.

- JDK 26 production installation with tests skipped
- JDK 26 compilation of public API crosscheck and exhaustive test classes
- focused execution on JDK 21 of the precompiled `Utf8InputScannerTest`, `Utf8CrosscheckTest`, `SweepJsonTest`, and work-counter `Utf8LinearTimeTest`, with Vector enabled

items.title: feat(benchmark): Haiku configs, perturbation probe, Python 3.14 fixes, context-limit handling
items.body:
## Context

All prior `claude-harness` benchmark results were **invalid** due to a HITL (Human-in-the-Loop) gate bug: harness agents correctly diagnosed bugs and produced accurate plans, but then waited for user confirmation before editing files. In an automated benchmark, no confirmation ever comes — so agents scored 0 not because the harness failed, but because they were waiting for a human. This affected only the `claude-harness` condition; baseline and ECC were unaffected.

## What this PR fixes

- **HITL gate fix**: injects a `HITL OVERRIDE` paragraph via `--append-system-prompt` for `full_harness` and `full_harness_rtk` configs, explicitly authorizing file edits in batch mode. Applied in both `benchmark/clawbench_v2/adapters/claude_code.py` and `benchmark/harness-bench/scripts/run-case.mjs`.
- **Workspace cleanup fix** (`run-case.mjs`): the original cleanup was gated on `setup_pass` / `core` fields that don't exist in harness-bench v2's success-path result objects, so workspaces were never deleted on infra failures. Changed to unconditional delete after `result.json` is written — prevents ENOSPC crashes from 300-500MB orphaned workspaces (langflow, gitea).
- **Haiku model configs**: added `claude-haiku-no-harness`, `claude-haiku-full-harness`, `claude-haiku-full-harness-rtk`, `claude-haiku-ecc`; bumped all timeouts 300s→600s.
- **Perturbation probe** (`benchmark/probe/`): k-depth call-chain generator + AST identifier scrambler for a controlled harness comparison on synthetic tasks.
- **Context-limit / rate-limit classification**: `classify_claude_failure` and `classify_codex_failure` now tag these correctly and mark `ok=False` even when exit code is clean.
- **Python 3.14 fix**: patched ISO-8859-1 typo in SWE pylint oracles.
- **Deterministic analysis** (`benchmark/analysis/summarise.py`): best-attempt scoring across all runs, difficulty-tier breakdown, bootstrap CI. Reproducible with `python3 benchmark/analysis/summarise.py`.
- **Observatory benchmark panel**: live `/api/benchmark` endpoint + `BenchmarkPanel` React component showing the 3-way comparison (baseline / harness / ECC) with difficulty breakdown.

## Post-fix benchmark results

Full writeup: `benchmark/harness-bench/benchmark/experiments/native-harness-hitl-rerun-2026-06-26/FINDINGS.md`

### Overall pass rate (27 cases, 3 conditions)

| Model | Baseline | Harness | ECC | Harness Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Haiku | 33% (9/27) | 41% (11/27) | 26% (7/27) | +7.4 pp |
| Sonnet | 59% (16/27) | 56% (15/27) | 48% (13/27) | -3.7 pp |

Bootstrap 95% CI includes 0 for both models — not statistically significant at n=27.

### By difficulty tier

| Difficulty | Haiku baseline | Haiku harness | Δ | Sonnet baseline | Sonnet harness | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 78% | 78% | 0 pp | 89% | 78% | -11 pp |
| Mid | 22% | 22% | 0 pp | 33% | 22% | -11 pp |
| High | 0% | 22% | **+22 pp** | 56% | 67% | **+11 pp** |

**Key finding:** harness value is task-complexity-dependent. On high-difficulty bugs the multi-agent pipeline (debugger → planner → implementer → reviewer → verifier) prevents premature fixes and the reviewers catch implementation mistakes. On easy bugs the TDD mandate and structured handoffs are overhead — the baseline explores more freely and finds the fix faster.

## What is NOT in this PR

`benchmark/harness-bench/` is a **nested git repository** with its own `.git`. The main repo sees it as an untracked directory, so the `run-case.mjs` cleanup fix and `FINDINGS.md` inside it are not tracked here — they exist locally and in the harness-bench repo only. items.body:
Follow-up to #279, fixing a class of hole I found in my own code just as that PR merged.

## The problem

A failed call is small, fast, and cheap to serve — so it **improves every axis the benchmark tracks**. A 500 on `/api/ingredients` would have turned 126,263 bytes into a few hundred, and `--fail-on-regression` would have reported a 99% improvement and exited 0.

Three instances, all the same shape:

| | what happened | why it was invisible |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **REST non-2xx** | recorded as a real measurement | the report tagged the status in the label, but nothing failed |
| **MCP tool errors** | recorded as a smaller payload | a failed tool returns HTTP **200** with `isError` on the result |
| **`recipes/{id}`** | 404 on any remote run | the path hard-coded the fixture's recipe id, which exists only in-process |

The third meant `--url` mode — the whole point of which is real-world numbers — was silently timing an error page for that endpoint.

## The fix

`McpCallResult.IsToolError` detects the MCP case. The recipe id is resolved from `/api/recipes?page=1&pageSize=1`, which is valid in both modes and deterministic in-process (the list order is fixed by the fixture's timestamps). A run that hits any failure prints what failed and **exits 3** without comparing against the baseline:

```text
This run measured failed calls, so its numbers are not comparable:
  GET /api/pantry-does-not-exist (pantry) returned HTTP 404
```

Exit codes are now **1** regression, **2** bad arguments, **3** invalid run.

## Verification

Pointed an endpoint at a missing path and confirmed exit 3 with the offending call named, then reverted. `dotnet test Kotlet.slnx` — 419 passed, 0 failed. Two consecutive clean runs produce identical bytes and query counts.

## One number moved

Resolving the recipe id changes *which* recipe is measured — the list is ordered by update time, so it resolves to the last fixture recipe rather than the first, and that one has no `sourceUrl`. `recipes/{id}` goes 2,413 → 2,399 bytes, and the API total 148,705 → 148,691. Baseline re-recorded; schema unchanged, so a v2 baseline still loads.

items.title: fix: stop a broker blip exhausting login ladders, and subscribe to contract-change events instead of polling
items.body:
## Summary

Three fixes from field-verifying `fb71b840` on THESHOW over 15 h, plus the root
cause of the one finding that fix did not close: the login ladder ignored the
SDK's own busy signal, the drift-burst gate was driven by the thinnest book on
the system, the contract-freshness gauge was structurally unable to fire an
alert, and the hourly contract poll was synthesising a signal the broker already
pushes.

**Already deployed to THESHOW and field-verified** — see the verification table.

## 1. The login ladder ignored the SDK's own busy signal (`524b4f94`)

On 2026-07-30 04:12 CST all six solace sessions dropped at once ("keep-alive on
tcp_TxRx detected session down"). The SDK went busy inside its own reconnect and
returned a raw `Already borrowed`. `SDKBusyError` is raised only by the
`InflightGuard`, which knows about workers *we* abandoned — it cannot see
shioaji's own internals holding the borrow. So the ladder skipped its busy
branch and drove the no-contract fallback and both retries into the same busy
object: **165 instant failures and 6 exhausted login ladders in 90 s, from one
upstream blip**.

`classify_login_failure` already mapped that string to `sdk_busy` for the metric.
The ladder just never consulted it. Now either source defers.

*The generalisable lesson: grep for **who reads** a classification, not whether
one exists.*

## 2. The drift-burst reference symbol was still chosen arbitrarily (`524b4f94`)

`fb71b840` latched the symbol, which fixed the *rotation* but not the *choice*.
Production latched **`EXFH6`** — a far-month contract quoting a **48-point
spread** — so the thinnest book on the system drove a platform-wide toxicity
gate (~346 bursts/day).

Now picks the tightest **relative** spread, compared by integer
cross-multiplication (core law 4 — no hot-path float price math). A non-positive
spread is a locked/half-built book and cannot outrank a real two-sided quote,
with a fallback so the gate is never silently starved of input.

## 3. `contract_cache_last_success_ts` was permanently 0.0 (`524b4f94`)

Which made `ContractCacheStale` (guarded on `> 0`) structurally unable to fire.
`fetch_contracts` fails 100% of the time (below), so the hourly refresh never
wrote the cache. Contract loading *at login* does work, so freshness is recorded
there — keyed on `login_fetch_contract`, **not** on `contracts_ready`
(`hasattr(api, "Contracts")`, always True once logged in; trusting that was the
original bug).

## 4. We were polling for a signal the broker already pushes (`1d2b29bd`)

The hourly contract refresh has **never** succeeded — 56/56 failures, every
cycle since the metrics begin, with `fetch_contracts: exclusive access lost`.

The mechanism is in the SDK binary, not in our code: 1.5.x `fetch_contracts`
needs sole ownership of the inner client (`Cannot logout: unexpected extra Arc
references`), and our facades hold **74 subscriptions plus registered callbacks
for the whole session**. Exclusivity is never obtainable. It fails identically
between sessions with streams idle, which is why every "contention" theory —
including my own earlier diagnosis — was wrong. **The 2 s stagger `fb71b840`
added is the evidence that hypothesis was wrong**: the facades demonstrably stop
contending, and the failure is unchanged.

So it cannot be patched. But shioaji 1.5.6 exposes `set_contract_event_callback`,
delivering `ContractUpdateEvent(action=FORCE|CHECK, security_type,
check_file_ts)` off the solace topic `APISUB/V1/SYS/CONTRACT`. **This repo had
never referenced it** (`grep set_contract_event_callback src/ tests/` → no hits).

This PR registers it, and **records only**:

- `contract_update_events_total{action,security_type}` and
  `contract_update_last_event_ts`. The gap between the latter and
  `contract_cache_last_success_ts` is the real staleness signal — when the broker
  last said contracts changed vs when we last loaded them.
- Labels bounded to the SDK's declared enum variants; unrecognised values
  collapse to `other` rather than minting series. Same discipline as
  `classify_login_failure`.
- The handler deliberately **does not fetch**. Re-entering the SDK from its own
  callback thread is exactly the `Already borrowed` re-entry behind finding 1,
  and it could not succeed anyway.
- Registration failure is non-fatal; contracts still load at login.

### Deliberately stops short of reacting to the event

Whether the SDK refreshes its own contract cache on `SYS/CONTRACT` or merely
notifies **cannot be determined from the binary** — it needs one live session.
Recording first makes that answer observable rather than guessed, and every
candidate design needs this signal regardless. Watch whether `action` arrives as
`FORCE` or `CHECK`: `CHECK` implies the SDK expects *us* to compare
`check_file_ts`.

### Correction to an option I previously put forward

`login(..., force_refresh=True)` does **not** refresh contracts. The adjacent
binary strings place it on the auth token cache (`force_refresh requested,
skipping cached token acquire`, under `api/v1/auth/token_login`). That option was
read from the flag's name rather than its neighbours, and is struck.

## Test Plan

- [x] Unit tests added/updated — 4 new test modules, behavioural tests confirmed to fail pre-fix
- [ ] Benchmark results reviewed — not latency-relevant (login ladder, callback registration, once-per-book-change symbol latch)

```
14672 passed / 19 skipped, coverage 87.90% (floor 70%)
typecheck: Success, 127 files
ruff format + lint: clean
discipline: 50 warnings, 0 blocking
shioaji-guard: 3 passed
dependency-boundary: 3 kept / 0 broken
test-hygiene: clean
```

The behavioural tests were confirmed to **fail against the unfixed source** —
e.g. `test_contract_refresh_startup_registers_the_broker_contract_event_callback`
fails pre-fix with `AssertionError: Expected 'set_contract_event_callback' to
have been called once. Called 0 times.`

**Not run:** `make ci` end-to-end, integration/e2e/benchmark.

## Field verification on THESHOW (deployed 2026-07-30 14:58Z, night session)

| Finding | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 3 — freshness gauge | **VERIFIED** | `contract_cache_last_success_ts 1785423581` — non-zero for the first time; it was `0.0` for the whole preceding 23 h container life |
| 4 — callback registers | **VERIFIED** | 4× `Contract event callback registered` at 14:59:42–44Z, one per facade |
| 4 — metric live | **VERIFIED** | `contract_update_last_event_ts` present (0.0 — no announcement yet; may take up to a day) |
| 2 — drift-burst symbol | **VERIFIED** | `drift_burst_reference_symbol_changed symbol=MXFH6 spread_scaled=20000` (2.0 pt) — was `EXFH6` at 48 pt |
| 1 — `sdk_busy` ladder | **NOT YET PROVEN** | Only exercised by a real broker blip. `Already borrowed` count is 0 since restart, which is absence of the trigger, not proof of the fix |
| Health floor | **VERIFIED** | 4/4 `logged_in 1`, `subscribed_count 74` each; 0 firing alerts; `hft_quote_pool_metrics_publish_errors_total 0`; ClickHouse ingest continuous (20,595 rows in 3 min) |
| Restart signature | **AS DOCUMENTED** | Exactly one broker 451 on one facade at 14:58:21Z, recovered at 14:59:42Z after the connection-limit backoff |

THESHOW stays `HFT_ORDER_MODE=sim` / `HFT_GATEWAY_ENABLED=0` — no live trading
anywhere in this change.

## Residual, named not dropped

The alert stanzas `ContractCacheStale` and `ContractRefreshFetchFailing` are
**still absent from the host** (79 rules). `config/monitoring/alerts/rules.yaml`
is host-authoritative and must be hand-merged on THESHOW with
`promtool check rules`, not shipped by file copy. Finding 3 is what makes
`ContractCacheStale` able to fire at all — until that stanza lands, the fixed
gauge has no alert reading it.

Three small, independent, low-risk performance fixes from the 2026-07-25
tokenize-speed investigation (19 findings total; this PR covers the

following #800/#801 which fixed the top-priority O(n^2) bug).

- **#807**: `Lattice::set_capacity`/`set_capacity_nbest` cleared
  `ends_at`/`all_paths` twice per call — `self.clear()` already does it;
  the second loop was provably dead work. Deleted it.
- **#804**: `Lattice::set_text`/`set_text_nbest`'s Aho-Corasick match
  pre-scan buffers (`matches_head`, `matches_store`) were local
  variables, freshly heap-allocated on every call, unlike every other

  per sentence (not once per document), so this churn compounds across a

- **#802**: `Token::get_detail()` allocated a full `Vec<&str>`

## Summary

Fixes the benchmarking result-integrity findings from `doc/code-findings.adoc` (#526):

- **H-4** — JFR event metadata (payload size, success/error labels, issuer) now describes the token actually validated; previously ~50% of Mixed-benchmark events were mislabeled because a second, independently randomized token was validated.
- **H-5** — No fabricated percentiles: the normal-distribution estimator is gone; reports contain only measured wrk percentiles, and the overview falls back to the wrk-reported average latency when P50 is absent.
- **H-6** — Failed runs now produce the intended F-grade report instead of crashing: `BenchmarkMetrics` accepts zero (still rejects negative), covered by an end-to-end null-overview report test.
- **H-7** — Performance score/grade computed in exactly one place (`MetricsComputer`), with the micro (JMH) and integration (wrk) formulas preserved numerically; the dead fourth grading scheme is deleted.
- **M-21** — The "expired token" benchmark now measures the expiry path (real issuer RSA key, past `exp`) instead of unknown-issuer rejection; error benchmarks throw if a known-bad token unexpectedly validates.
- **M-22** — Prometheus parsing keeps all series per metric; heap memory selects the `area="heap"` series and JWT counters aggregate across series instead of reading an arbitrary first series.

items.title: fix(benchmark): replace unverified dev benchmarks with real measured results
items.body:
## What & why

The first benchmark numbers were **dev placeholders I generated with an AI coding agent and shipped without verifying** — my fault, not a measured run. They extrapolated a 50-document sample via a scaling factor, used placeholder vectors, and reported trivially perfect precision on non-ambiguous synthetic names. None of it was actually measured.

This PR rips all of that out and replaces it with a **fully reproducible, honestly-measured** run. Lesson for anyone shipping AI-agent output: the numbers look plausible and confident — verify every metric before publishing.

## Real run (baseline, before the lexical layer)

500 docs / 3000 mentions / 63 identities. Default config, **no** `alias_map`:

| Metric | Naive | Full LLM ER | AutoGraft |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| LLM ER calls | 0 | 3000 | **238** (92.1% local) |
| Tokens | 0 | 661,714 | **52,496** |
| Cost | $0 | $0.0334 | **$0.00265** |
| Precision / Recall | — | — | **100% / 98.6%** |

> A follow-up (PR #26, the lexical layer) cuts LLM calls further (238 → 7) and lifts recall (98.6% → 99.4%). Current canonical numbers live in `BENCHMARK.md`. This PR is the **baseline**; the two snapshots are not a contradiction but the before/after of the lexical layer.

## Methodology
- **Corpus:** 63 real-world identities with authentic variants + 8 homonym traps, deterministic (seed 42), each mention carries a ground-truth `canonical_id`.
- **Embeddings:** real `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (CPU) — not placeholders.
- **Engine:** the actual `resolve_entity` pipeline (`ListDatabaseClient`).
- **LLM:** real Groq `groq/llama-3.1-8b-instant` arbiter calls, tokens read from API responses.
- **Pricing:** real `litellm.completion_cost` (published Groq prices).

## Honest limitations
- **40 missed merges** (recall 98.6%): stock tickers (`GOOGL`, `TSLA`, `GS`), full-name reversals (`British Petroleum`→`BP`, `World Health Organization`→`WHO`). Below the cosine uncertainty threshold, never reach the LLM — a real trade-off, not a bug.
- Homonym isolation works perfectly (Apple fruit vs company: 0 cross-contamination).

## Reproduce
`PYTHONPATH=. python3 benchmark/run_real_benchmark.py` (~9 min, real API calls). Full per-mention audit data in `benchmark/assets/real_benchmark_results.json`.

items.body:
Two small `roi_slack.py` fixes to the ROI companion table.

## 1. Flag stale ROI results instead of posting them as current

The ROI companion posts stale data as current when `roi_sim` silently fails — the realistic failure mode bypasses #397's `_load_results` WARNING entirely:

1. `benchmark_flywheel.yaml`'s *Download previous benchmark data* step restores the **previous run's** `roi_results.json` into `benchmark/results/` before `roi_sim` runs.
2. The *Simulate trader ROI* step is `continue-on-error: true`, and `roi_sim.main()` hard-exits before `write_outputs()` on artifact drift.

Net: the file is yesterday's (or older) — **valid JSON**, so `_load_results` parses it, `build_roi_section` renders it, and the section keeps posting the same numbers looking current. No log line, no freshness indicator (only relative `window_days` is rendered, never `as_of`/`window_end`).

- **Freshness guard:** `build_roi_section` compares `as_of` (else `window_end`) against now. Past `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` (2.0 ≈ 2× daily cadence) it logs a WARNING and stamps a visible `*(stale — as of YYYY-MM-DD)*` marker. Marking (not suppressing) keeps the numbers visible but flagged — suppression would again be indistinguishable from "no data yet".
- **Malformed `groups`:** a missing / wrong-typed `groups` key now WARNs instead of returning `None` silently.
- Tests for both, plus the quiet-on-missing / warn-on-broken `_load_results` split. The shared `_write_results` fixture now defaults `as_of` to today so freshness-agnostic tests stay current.

## 2. Never truncate tool names

The `MAX_LINE_WIDTH=160` backstop shrank the **tool** column (down to `_TOOL_MIN`) on realistic tables, cutting `superforcaster_calibrated_full_search` → `superforcaster_calibra…` and `predict-fine-tuned-calibrated` → `predict-fine-tuned-cal…`. Slack code blocks scroll horizontally (the module's own rationale), so:

- The tool column is uncapped (`_CAPS[0] = None`) and never shrunk; `_TOOL_CAP` / `_TOOL_MIN` removed.
- The `MAX_LINE_WIDTH` backstop now only shrinks the free-form **flags** column.
- `TestLineWidth` updated to the new contract (a long tool name renders in full).

## Checks

`black / isort / flake8 / darglint / mypy / pylint` clean; 54 `test_roi_slack.py` pass.

## Note

Builds on #397 (the `roi_slack` logger + the `_load_results` WARNING). #397's head branch is not present on origin, so this PR is opened against `main`; the #397 commits shown here collapse to just these two commits once #397 merges. Follow-up to the #397 review discussion.

## The bug

`AFTQueryAppraisedEsmemAdapter.ingest` built a temporary `EmotionalMemory` sharing `self._appraiser` and called `engine.close()` — which closes the appraisal engine's **httpx client**. Every subsequent `retrieve()`-time query appraisal hit a closed client and, with `fallback_on_error=True`, **silently fell back to the keyword appraiser** instead of the pre-registered `DIRECT_VAD_SCHEMA`. ~1,131 of ~1,133 query appraisals were affected (session/encode appraisals ran before the close → D1/D2 valid). MADial-Bench (Addendum X) is unaffected (persistent engine).

## The fix

- `ingest` no longer closes the engine (InMemoryStore is GC'd; the shared appraiser stays open); a new `close()` releases the appraiser once at end of run, mirroring the MADial adapter.

## Data correction (X2 re-run with genuine direct-VAD)

Verdict **unchanged** (Hx2 FAIL, inverted, powered); magnitude modestly smaller — direct-VAD query affect is slightly less harmful than keyword on this affect-orthogonal corpus:

| AFT u_nDCG@4 | 0.120 | **0.133** |
| Δ | −0.164 | **−0.150** [−0.165, −0.136] |

items.title: Fix benchmark results: detect unconditional auto-configurations during training
items.body:
The benchmark's optimized run produced no results because the optimizer crashed the app at startup. `detectLoadedAutoConfigurations()` missed auto-configurations without class-level conditions (e.g. `EndpointAutoConfiguration`) — these appear only as `ClassName#methodName` method-level entries in `ConditionEvaluationReport`, never as top-level keys. The optimizer then excluded them, causing `ParameterValueMapper` to be unavailable and `WebEndpointAutoConfiguration` to fail.

## Description

**Three fixes:**

### 1. Training detection bug (`TrainingRunApplicationListener`)

`ConditionEvaluationReport` stores two key formats:
- Class-level: `org.springframework.boot.actuate.autoconfigure.endpoint.EndpointAutoConfiguration` (only present when the class has `@Conditional*` annotations)
- Method-level: `…EndpointAutoConfiguration#endpointOperationParameterMapper` (always present for `@Bean` method conditions)

Old code only matched class-level keys. Fix iterates available auto-configs and accepts either a class-level `isFullMatch()=true` **or** any method-level entry for that class:

```java
// Extract class names from "ClassName#methodName" entries
Set<String> classesFromMethodEntries = conditionOutcomes.keySet().stream()
    .filter(key -> key.contains("#"))
    .map(key -> key.substring(0, key.indexOf('#')))
    .collect(Collectors.toSet());

return availableAutoConfigs.stream().filter(config -> {
    ConditionEvaluationReport.ConditionAndOutcomes outcomes = conditionOutcomes.get(config);
    if (outcomes != null) {
        return outcomes.isFullMatch();          // class-level condition matched
    }
    return classesFromMethodEntries.contains(config); // unconditionally loaded
}).sorted().collect(Collectors.toList());
```

Two new unit tests cover the method-level detection and the negative (failed class-level condition) case.

### 2. Benchmark measurement loop (`.github/workflows/benchmarks.yml`)

`grep -m1 | timeout` left the JVM running for the full 60s timeout per iteration (Java ignores SIGPIPE), making the baseline step take ~5 minutes. Replaced with a background process + temp file polling loop that kills the JVM immediately after capturing the startup line.

### 3. Shade plugin warnings (`benchmarks/pom.xml`)

Added `module-info.class` filter and `AppendingTransformer` entries for `spring.handlers`, `spring.schemas`, `spring.tooling`, `spring.factories`, and `spring/aot.factories` to silence overlapping-resource warnings.

items.title: [CUDA] Fuse MoE finalize into FC2 GEMV and skip expandInputRows
items.body:
## Description

At decode (one token per sequence) the int4/int8 QMoE path launches six kernels per layer, two of
which move data rather than compute: `expandInputRows` gathers each token into `top_k` permuted
copies before FC1, and `finalizeMoeRouting` scatter-reduces those copies back afterwards. On a
small GPU this is pure overhead — the MoE GEMVs themselves are already at ~94% of the measured DRAM
roofline, so the remaining headroom is in the prologue/epilogue, not the math.

This PR removes both kernels for the decode-shaped GEMV path: the finalize reduction is folded into
the FC2 GEMV epilogue, and FC1 reads the unexpanded activations directly through the existing
permutation map. Measured **+2.5% decode throughput** on gpt-oss-20b (int4) / RTX 5060 Ti. Both
optimizations are gated behind support predicates and environment kill switches, and neither
changes behavior for shapes outside the GEMV's profiled range.

## Summary of Changes

### 1. Fuse the MoE finalize into the FC2 GEMV epilogue

`moe_gemv_fused_finalize_kernel` launches one block per `(token, n-tile)` and loops over the
token's `experts_per_token` permuted rows, accumulating `row_scale * (dot + bias)` into a shared
float accumulator before a single store. This replaces the separate
`finalizeMoeRoutingKernelLauncher` pass, which re-read the FC2 output from global memory.

- Gated by `is_moe_gemv_fused_finalize_supported()`, which additionally requires
  `num_rows * experts_per_token == expanded_num_rows` (i.e. no dropped tokens) on top of the
  existing GEMV shape checks.
- Restricted to `OutputType == T`; the mixed-output-type and TMA-warp-specialized paths keep the
  old two-kernel flow.
- Kill switch: `ORT_DISABLE_MOE_GEMV_FUSED_FINALIZE=1`.

### 2. Skip `expandInputRows` when the FC1 GEMV runs

The FC1 interleaved-SwiGLU GEMV now takes an optional `permuted_row_to_source_row` map and resolves
its activation row as `permuted_row_to_source_row[row] % num_rows`, so the expanded activation
buffer never has to be materialized. Only the *activation iterator* is redirected — the output
pointer still uses the permuted row index, so the FC1 output layout is unchanged.

- `runMoe` decides this *before* `gemm1` runs, so the predicate must exactly match the one `gemm1`
  uses to select the GEMV. Both call the shared `moeGemvInterleavedSwiGLUWillRun()` /
  `MoeGemvFc1Disabled()` helpers rather than open-coding the condition, and an `ORT_ENFORCE` in
  `gemm1` catches any future divergence instead of silently computing on unexpanded data.
- Only applies when the expansion would be a pure permutation (no FP4/FP8/AWQ/prequant-scale or
  per-expert activation scale variants).
- Kill switch: `ORT_DISABLE_MOE_GEMV_SKIP_EXPAND=1`.

### 3. Supporting cleanup and test coverage

- `is_moe_gemv_shape_supported(..., cta_n)` factors out the shared shape checks with the n-tiling
  requirement parameterized. The plain GEMVs pass `kCtaN`; the fused-finalize path passes the
  smaller `kFusedFinalizeCtaN` that its `grid.y` actually depends on, instead of inheriting the
  stricter constraint and then redundantly re-checking the looser one.
- `quant_dequant_blockwise()` no longer emits an all-128 zero-point tensor for symmetric 8-bit. The
  offset is already baked into the weight converter, so the tensor was a numerical no-op — but it
  made `weight_zeros` non-null, and every MoE GEMV entry point rejects block-wise cases with
  non-null zeros. It was silently keeping all block-wise 8-bit configs off the GEMV.

## Benchmark results

gpt-oss-20b int4, RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120, 16 GB) on WSL2, CUDA 13.0, CUDA graph enabled.
`batch=1, prompt=512, gen=128, reps=5`, 5 interleaved passes. Arms are selected with the
environment kill switches on a **single binary**, so the only variable is the code path taken.

| Variant | TTFT (ms) | Token latency (ms) | Decode (tps) | vs. baseline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Neither optimization (baseline) | 122.17 | 6.398 | 156.31 | — |
| Skip-expand only | 121.79 | 6.358 | 157.31 | +0.6% |
| Both (this PR) | 122.37 | 6.242 | **160.23** | **+2.5%** |

Per-pass decode tps (paired — same pass means same thermal/clock conditions):

| Pass | none | skip-expand | both |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 157.10 | 158.27 | 162.94 |
| 2 | 156.10 | 158.35 | 160.11 |
| 3 | 157.07 | 153.66 | 157.58 |
| 4 | 156.07 | 157.99 | 159.43 |
| 5 | 155.21 | 158.30 | 161.08 |

Notes on interpretation:

- "Both vs. neither" wins **5/5** paired passes (+2.5% mean), so the combined result is solid.
- The **fused finalize is the larger contributor** (+1.9%, 5/5 paired wins over the skip-expand-only
  arm). **Skip-expand alone is +0.6%, which is at this harness's ~0.5% noise floor** (4/5 paired
  wins, and pass 3 is negative). It is worth keeping as a strict kernel-count reduction, but it
  should not be sold as a measurable win on its own.
- TTFT is unchanged, as expected — prefill uses the grouped GEMM and neither path is touched.
- Single machine, single model. GPUs where the MoE GEMV is not selected at all will see no change.

`test_swiglu_qmoe_gemv_parity` is new and is the only test that actually reaches the MoE GEMV:
`is_moe_gemv_supported` requires every GEMM dim `>= 512`, while every pre-existing functional QMoE
config uses `hidden_size=128, intermediate_size=256` and therefore exercises the CUTLASS grouped
GEMM. The new case uses `hidden_size = intermediate_size = 512` with `num_experts_per_token = 4`,
so FC1 sees `n=1024, k=512` and FC2 sees `n=512, k=512`; `batch * seq` of 1 and 2 gives 4 and 8
expanded rows, covering both sides of `kMaxProfiledExpandedRowsForSmallProblemDim`. The 2-token
cases are what exercise the multi-token index math in both new code paths, which degenerates to a
no-op when `num_rows == 1`.

Coverage was verified by temporarily placing a conditional `ORT_ENFORCE` immediately before each
GEMV launch and confirming which tests tripped it — armed one path at a time, since an FC1 throw
preempts FC2. All 7 new cases reach both the FC1 GEMV and the FC2 fused finalize; no pre-existing
test reached either.

## Motivation and Context

Profiling gpt-oss-20b decode on an RTX 5060 Ti attributes ~86% of decode time to QMoE. Modelling
QMoE cost against bytes moved gives a slope of 2.748 µs/MiB (= 382 GB/s against a measured 427 GB/s
sustained roofline) with a fixed ~120 µs intercept; after subtracting host-side `Run()` overhead
that leaves ~41 µs per call of non-GEMV GPU work. That intercept, not the GEMV, is what this PR
targets. Kernels per int4 QMoE decode call drop from six to four.

One further prologue fusion was implemented and measured on this branch (folding softmax/top-k into
the expert-map kernel, commits `2a1d49b4e8` / `67e67e1302`) and produced +0.24% — indistinguishable
from noise at p≈0.23 over 7 passes — so it was reverted rather than kept. The launch-latency floor
for the remaining prologue kernels appears to have been reached. The net diff of this branch
contains only the two optimizations described above.
